questions.question: Image A numbers the elements in the order keyboard focus reaches them (1 first); input.image_shows says which part of the page it shows. input.order lists every element with role, name, position and form group, and input.signals lists where the order departs from the reading order. When input.backward is given, the Shift+Tab order differs from the reverse of the forward order: judge it too (it need not mirror the forward order, but it must also make sense). When input.opened is given, it lists what a menu or disclosure revealed and where the next Tab went. Would a keyboard user meet these elements in an order that makes sense for reading and using this part of the page? Answer preserves, does_not_preserve, does_not_matter (order cannot affect meaning here), or unsure, and give your reasons in a few plain words. An element in input.order marked drawn: false has no visible box (it is hidden, off the page, tiny, or shown only while it has focus), so image A has no number for it: judge it from input.order alone.
questions.rubric: The question is whether the order keeps the page's meaning and lets a keyboard user operate it, not whether it matches the order drawn on the screen: an order that differs from the drawn one is not does_not_preserve by itself. does_not_preserve: related fields split apart (the address fields interleaved with other fields); numbered steps, or any items whose order is the point (a timeline, a form's fields), reached out of sequence; a Shift+Tab order that jumps around so going back makes no sense; focus jumping back and forth between unrelated areas; a menu's or dialog's content reached far from its trigger; a positive tabindex sending focus to an unrelated place first. preserves: columns read one after another; a grid of cards, or columns of footer links, read row by row with each card's or item's parts together (its image link, then its title link); tiles in a row or a slider reached from right to left or left to right when each tile is independent and its own parts stay together; one tile's own buttons reached in another order than drawn (a Share button before its Save button); a side list's sub-items reached right after their parent item; main content reached before side navigation that comes later in the document; header, navigation, main, footer; a skip link first; independent sidebars in either order. does_not_matter: independent items whose order cannot change meaning, such as a row of social media icons. unsure: whenever the evidence does not settle it (the image does not show the numbered elements the signals name clearly; the grouping that matters is not visible; you cannot tell whether the items are independent or a sequence; the content is in a language you cannot read). questions.question: Image A shows the field in input.field while it has focus, with what is around it. Is there visible text or a picture next to it that is this field's label or instructions (whether they are accurate is another test)? Answer labeled (copy the words from input.text, input.buttons_next_to_it or input.labels_of_neighbouring_fields into quote), graphic (describe it in reasons), not_labeled or unsure.
questions.rubric: labeled: text people can see, beside, above or inside the field while it has focus, that goes with it as its label or instructions, accurate or not ("First Name:" next to it, a column heading over a grid of fields, one label for a set of phone number boxes, a button beside a box). A button in input.buttons_next_to_it counts, whatever its words, when it belongs with this field: the box's own button, beside it or just under it in a form of one field; whether its words describe the field is not asked here. A form's submit button below a form of several fields labels none of them, so such a field with nothing else is not_labeled. A label in input.labels_of_neighbouring_fields counts only when this field is part of the set it labels (the second and third boxes of one phone number). For a radio button or checkbox, input.question_of_the_set (a legend over several options) does not label it: the option needs its own words or picture, or a person cannot tell the choices apart. graphic: a picture that plainly labels it (a magnifier on a search box). not_labeled: nothing visible relates to the field. questions.rubric: descriptive: names what to enter or do, even in one word ("First name", "Search" next to a search box, "Name" under a visible "Billing address" heading or group label). not descriptive: unrelated or empty of meaning ("Menu", "Info", "The sky is blue", "Field 1"), the same label on several fields with nothing visible to tell them apart, a date or number field whose required format appears only in an error message.
